opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think there's something right about that, and it's very much an engineer's way of thinking. Feynman had that line on his blackboard, "What I cannot create, I do not understand," and I resonate with it. If you can take a system apart and put it back together out of pieces you actually understand, pieces whose properties you can reason about, then you've got a kind of understanding that's more than just a description. You can predict, you can modify, you can fix it when it breaks.

But I'd add a couple of caveats. First, the building blocks matter enormously, and they're not God-given. In my own career I've moved among different sets of building blocks: graphical models, optimization, sampling, statistical inference, and increasingly ideas from economics like incentives, mechanisms, and contracts. Each set gives you a different perspective on the same phenomenon. So "reconstructing from your own perspective" is honest about the fact that it's *a* perspective. Someone else, with a different toolbox, might reconstruct it differently and see things you miss. That's healthy, not a problem.

Second, a lot of the systems we care about now aren't single artifacts. They're collectives: markets, networks of people and algorithms interacting, data flowing among agents with their own goals. You can't understand those just by building a bigger and bigger model of one brain or one neural net. You need building blocks that talk about interaction, uncertainty, and incentives. That's where I think the current AI conversation is a bit impoverished. We keep trying to understand intelligence by building one giant thing that imitates a human, when a lot of real intelligence, the kind that feeds cities and allocates resources, is in the system level, in the collective.

And third, I'd say that understanding in the engineering sense has to include guarantees. It's not enough to build something that works on the examples you tried. You want to be able to say: under these assumptions, with this much data, here's how wrong I could be. That's what statistics has always brought to the table. So, yes, reconstruction from building blocks, but with blocks that let you reason about error, uncertainty, and consequences when the thing is deployed in the real world among real people.

r002.rationale: The response says understanding enables prediction, modification, and repair, but does not state that trying alternatives and testing results can improve a system without understanding how it works.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think that's actually a pretty good description of what we do in science, and it's also a pretty good description of what I think learning is, in a broad sense. You don't understand something by having a picture of it handed to you. You understand it when you can take it apart and put it back together using pieces that you already have some command over. And the pieces matter. If I'm an engineer, my building blocks are things like feedback, stability, modularity, abstraction layers. If I'm a statistician, they're things like uncertainty, sampling, decision-making under incomplete information. Same system, different reconstruction, and both can be legitimate.

So I take the perspective-dependence seriously. I don't think there's a view from nowhere. When people say "we don't understand deep learning," what they usually mean is that one particular set of building blocks, say classical statistical learning theory, doesn't reassemble the phenomenon cleanly. That's a real gap, but it's not the same as saying nothing is understood. Somebody with an optimization background reconstructs it one way, somebody with a physics background another way, and the field's understanding is the union of those reconstructions, plus the friction between them.

Where I get a little wary is when people confuse reconstructing a system with mimicking its surface. A model that reproduces outputs is not the same as a model built from components you can reason about independently. In engineering, we care that the parts have contracts. I can swap a component, I know what breaks and what doesn't. That's the kind of understanding that lets you build things that work at scale and that other people can trust. A lot of the current excitement is about systems that are impressive but don't yet decompose that way, and so our "understanding" of them is still mostly empirical, closer to natural history than to engineering.

And then the last piece for me is that the building blocks shouldn't only be about the individual learner or the individual model. The systems I'm most interested in are collective ones: markets, networks of agents, people and algorithms interacting with incentives and incomplete information. If your blocks are only neurons and gradients, you'll reconstruct a brain-like thing. If your blocks include contracts, prices, and the fact that different parties know different things, you reconstruct something that looks more like an economy. I happen to think the second set of blocks is where a lot of the real-world value and the real-world risk is going to be, and it's been underweighted in how the field talks about intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response discusses reconstructing systems through different conceptual building blocks, but does not say researchers translate the idea into an equilibrium or optimization problem.

r002.rationale: It contrasts empirical performance with decomposable understanding, but does not state that trying alternatives and testing results can improve a system without explaining how it works.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a useful way to approach understanding, provided you don’t confuse your reconstruction with the system itself. You choose building blocks, you decide which relationships matter, and you try to put them together in a way that explains what you observe. Those choices reflect your perspective and the questions you’re asking.

But I would want to go beyond being able to reconstruct something. Can I predict what happens when I change a component? Can I explain where my description breaks down? There may be several descriptions of the same system that are useful at different levels. Understanding doesn’t necessarily mean reducing everything to one privileged set of pieces.

And with a complex system, much of what matters is in the interactions. Knowing what each component does in isolation may tell you surprisingly little about what happens when they’re coupled together. So the building blocks are a starting point. The deeper question is whether you understand the principles governing how they work together.

r002.rationale: It asks whether one can predict outcomes after changing a component, but does not state that trying alternatives and testing results can improve a system without understanding how it works.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s part of what we mean by understanding. You take something complex and find a set of concepts that lets you reason about it, make predictions, and perhaps intervene. But I’d be careful about identifying understanding with reconstruction. You can reproduce the behavior of a system without having a particularly useful explanation of it.

The building blocks matter, and they depend on the questions you’re asking. If I’m trying to understand a market, I might think in terms of agents, information, incentives, and interactions. If I’m trying to understand an algorithm, I might think in terms of optimization and statistical uncertainty. Those are different perspectives, and neither has to capture every detail to be useful.

So the test, for me, is whether your perspective gives you some purchase on the system. Can you explain what happens when conditions change? Can you identify where your account breaks down? That’s where understanding becomes more than a reconstruction that makes sense to you.
